14, 4203) compared, per participant, how well a model with several latent states and a model with a single state explained shock-probability ratings in an aversive reversal-learning task. The difference in fit correlated with trait anxiety in the session with the most reliable outcomes (90/10 contingencies, r(36) = 0.39, CI [0.07, 0.63], p = .017, Fig. 6c). They found no association in the 75/25 and 60/40 sessions. This page applies the same logic to the TAMBI task. It asks whether the participants whose allocations are better predicted by a model with latent states than by a model with one direction per cue differ in their questionnaire scores.

The parameters are estimated by maximum likelihood (Nelder-Mead on a logit transform of the prior ranges, at most 400 evaluations per start). The starts are the BayesFlow posterior mean of the participant (for Nexus, Nassar and Zika) and three random draws from the priors.

Relative fit is cross-validated. The parameters are fitted on the odd episodes and evaluated on the even episodes, and vice versa. Beliefs are always replayed on the full trial sequence, so only the evaluation is split. The held-out log-likelihood of both folds is summed and divided by the number of held-out trials. The relative fit of a participant is the held-out log-likelihood per trial (nats) of a model with latent states minus that of a model without latent states. Positive values mean that the model with latent states predicts the held-out allocations better.
direct counterpart of Zika et al. (2023)

The 1-state model of Zika et al. learns one outcome probability with a count-based, decaying learning rate and has no mechanism for change-points. The tracker is the closest counterpart in the TAMBI task. The Nassar observer is a reference with change-point resets, which also produce fast relearning after a switch. The recovery below separates the n-state model from both references, and both comparisons are reported.

The held-out log-likelihood identifies the generating model in 84 % to 96 % of the data sets, and each relative-fit outcome is positive when the data come from the model with states it contains and mostly negative when they come from a reference. Two properties matter for the interpretation of the participant data. First,

is close to zero for data from the Nassar observer, so this outcome separates models with states from a model with a fixed learning rate but not from a model with change-point resets. Second, the relative fits of the participants (medians 0.02 to 0.10 nats per trial) are much smaller than those of data simulated from any of the models with states (medians 0.30 to 3.80). The participants’ allocations thus lie between the models, and relative fit grades how far a participant’s allocations lean toward a model with states. Relation to behavioural measures and parameters

children.label: Relation to behavioural measures and parameters

children.value: Spearman correlations of relative fit with the structural signatures, the state-selectivity measures, the coverage of the allocations and the Nexus BayesFlow parameters (96 participants, file

The relative fit of Nexus (against either reference) correlates with hedging between the trained directions after a transition (ρ = 0.52 and 0.53) and after an oddball (ρ = 0.62 and 0.63), with the mass of the allocation on the other learned state (ρ = 0.50 and 0.46) and on no learned state (ρ = 0.43 and 0.41), and with the Nexus parameters noise_reactivity (ρ = 0.40 and 0.42) and belief_momentum (ρ = 0.23 and 0.40). Nexus predicts those participants better whose nets are spread over more than one direction. The two references concentrate their allocation around one direction per cue and cannot produce such a spread.

The relative fit of the n-state model against the tracker correlates with the Nexus parameter h_switch (ρ = 0.36) and negatively with belief_momentum (ρ = −0.39), noise_reactivity (ρ = −0.26) and transfer_I_e_abs (ρ = −0.32). Against the Nassar observer it correlates with the noise weight of the state-selectivity model (ρ = −0.22).

the OCI slope became 0.23 [0.02, 0.44] (p = .034) with transfer, consolidation after transitions and snap-back after oddballs as covariates.

Across the three instruction conditions the advantage of a model with latent states over a model with one direction per cue was unrelated to the general factor (slopes −0.12 to 0.17) and, with one exception (OCI with Nexus against the tracker, 0.21, p = .047), to the five scales. This holds for both models with states, for both references, with and without the reference fit as covariate, and for the direct counterpart of the analysis of Zika et al. (2023). With 95 participants the power to detect a correlation of 0.39 at α = .05 (two-sided) is .98, and that to detect a correlation of 0.2 is .49. A correlation of the size reported by Zika et al. would therefore very likely have been detected, whereas smaller associations cannot be excluded.

In Full, higher OCI and general-factor scores went with a better fit of Nexus relative to the references, and higher STICSA trait and general-factor scores with a worse fit of the n-state model relative to the Nassar observer. The Nexus slopes in Full depend on two participants with high OCI scores whose allocations Nexus predicts far better than any other participant’s; the rank correlations keep the OCI association with

The relative fit of Nexus is largely accounted for by how much a participant hedges between learned directions (61 to 67 % of its variance by three behavioural measures). It is therefore a model-based summary of behaviour that the structural signatures already measure and not an independent measure of state inference.
